summary: Discusses the philosophy and implementation of the ready line in the Host-IMP interface. BBN Report 1822 defines the interface, and this note comes from a committee working on standardizing PDP-11 local host interfaces.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 642 explains how a host interface should respond when the ready signal between a Host and an IMP drops. It recommends discarding any message in progress and restarting after the signal has stabilized.

questions: what is the imp ready line
what happens when the host imp ready line drops
how long should the host wait after raising the ready line
subtitle: How the Host-IMP ready lines help an interface discard incomplete messages and restart safely.

tldr.problem: BBN Report 1822 described the IMP side of the Host-IMP interface but left some recommended host behavior implicit, leading to confusion among implementors.
tldr.mechanism: A drop in either ready line sets error status; the interface discards messages in progress and uses separate input and output processes to resume after the line stabilizes.
tldr.outcome: RFC 642 gives implementors a recommended procedure for resynchronizing message flow without involving the NCP in the ready-line recovery.

today: The unit records RFC 642's status as Unknown and lists no updates or obsoleting RFCs. It describes a recommendation for the ARPANET Host-IMP interface.

sections.title: Making the Ready-Line Guidance Explicit
sections.content:
BBN Report 1822 specifies the Host-IMP interface, but focuses on the IMP's implementation and suggests that the host behave similarly. A committee reviewing PDP-11 host interfaces found confusion about what that meant in practice.

RFC 642 makes the recommendations explicit as a guide for interface implementors. Its goals are to restore communication reliably after temporary service loss and to keep host interface programming simple.
sections.plainLanguage: The interface report did not spell out every step for the host side. This memo gives implementors a consistent way to handle the ready signal.

sections.title: Discarding Messages After a Ready-Line Drop
sections.content:
When the IMP ready line drops, either message in transit may be incomplete. Both the Host and IMP must recognize this and discard the message being received; the standard convention uses a Host-IMP NOP message intended to be thrown away.

The suggested host driver uses one process for input and another for output. A drop sets input and output error status, and the processes clear their errors independently. The input process flushes an incomplete message and reuses its buffer; the output process flushes an incomplete message rather than removing it as successfully sent.
sections.plainLanguage: If the ready signal drops during a message, the interface treats that message as incomplete and throws it away. Separate input and output processes then continue when the connection is ready again.

sections.title: Restarting and Stabilizing the Line
sections.content:
At system startup or restart, the host clears its READY flop, waits one-half second and sets it again. Starting the input and output processes then resynchronizes Host-IMP communication. The NCP is resynchronized separately by the type 10 IMP-to-host message “interface was reset.”

The host must also avoid transmitting while its own ready line is settling. The RFC permits hardware stabilization or a software wait of one-half second after setting the host ready flop. The ready-line errors should affect only the interface processes, not the NCP or connection database.
sections.plainLanguage: After raising its ready signal, the host waits one-half second before sending or receiving. The interface restarts its own processes, while the NCP receives a separate reset message.

references.text: RFC 636, cited for the effect of the IMP ready line on interface processes and the NCP.
